systems.name: Laissez-faire capitalism
systems.description: private ownership, minimal state (defense, courts, contract enforcement).

systems.name: Social-democratic capitalism
systems.description: private ownership and markets plus a large tax-funded state correcting failures and redistributing. Nordic model; the German variant adds codetermination.

systems.name: Market socialism / economic democracy
systems.description: worker-managed or socially-owned firms competing in markets. Schweickart's model, Yugoslav self-management, Mondragón-style cooperative federations.

systems.name: Central planning
systems.description: state ownership and administrative allocation without market prices. Soviet-type; computational planning is the modern variant.

systems.name: Social anarchism
systems.description: no state; production by federated worker associations or communes. Mutualism, collectivism, syndicalism, anarcho-communism. Spain 1936–39 is the main test; Ostrom's polycentric commons the closest documented small-scale analogue.

systems.name: State capitalism / developmental state
systems.description: markets and private firms, with the state steering credit, protecting strategic sectors, and owning key enterprises. Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan; China since 1978.

systems.name: Anarcho-capitalism
systems.description: no state; law, courts, and defense supplied by competing private agencies (Rothbard, David Friedman). No real-world case; medieval Iceland and Somalia 1991–2006 are the contested analogies.

systems.name: Participatory economics (Parecon)
systems.description: no markets, no state; worker and consumer councils, balanced job complexes, pay by effort, allocation by iterated participatory planning with indicative prices (Albert, Hahnel). No real-world case.

cruxes.title: Information and coordination
cruxes.prompt: How does the system know what to produce and where resources should go?
cruxes.verdictText: Laissez-faire, social democracy, state capitalism (for catch-up) — strong. Market socialism — strong on goods, weak on investment. Central planning — weak, with a strong negative record. Social anarchism — strong in mutualist form, untested otherwise. Anarcho-capitalism — strong on private goods, no answer for public ones. Parecon — untested; theoretically contested.

cruxes.title: Innovation, risk, and failure
cruxes.prompt: Who funds experiments, who bears risk, and what happens when something fails?
cruxes.verdictText: Laissez-faire, social democracy — strong. State capitalism — strong for catch-up, contested at the frontier. Market socialism — mixed. Central planning — weak outside priorities. Social anarchism, anarcho-capitalism, Parecon — untested.

cruxes.title: Ownership of production and control of surplus
cruxes.prompt: Who owns productive assets, who captures profit, and what is the status of wage labor?
cruxes.verdictText: Partly a value question. Market socialism, social anarchism, and Parecon eliminate the wage relation; social democracy moderates it; the others do not.

cruxes.title: Hierarchy and voice inside the workplace
cruxes.prompt: Who has authority over work, and how are decisions made?
cruxes.verdictText: Parecon, social anarchism, market socialism — strongest by design, all scale-limited. Social democracy — moderate. Laissez-faire, anarcho-capitalism, central planning, state capitalism — weak.

cruxes.title: Externalities and public goods
cruxes.prompt: How are costs and benefits not captured by prices handled?
cruxes.verdictText: Social democracy — strongest record. State capitalism — strong when willing, unaccountable when not. Market socialism — inherits social democracy's tools. Central planning — weak in practice. Social anarchism — local only. Laissez-faire, anarcho-capitalism — weak. Parecon — untested.

cruxes.title: Inequality and concentration of private capital
cruxes.prompt: What stops accumulation from becoming dynastic wealth and political power?
cruxes.verdictText: The structural solutions (market socialism, central planning, anarchism, Parecon) relocate concentration rather than eliminate it. Social democracy — mixed, erodes. State capitalism — concentrates in the state. Laissez-faire, anarcho-capitalism — weak.

cruxes.title: Concentration of state power and capture of the state
cruxes.prompt: What constrains the state, and what prevents the powerful from capturing it?
cruxes.verdictText: Social democracy — strongest record, capture unresolved. State capitalism — depends on elite discipline, no guarantee. Anarchism and anarcho-capitalism — remove the target, no answer to re-emergence. Central planning — worst. Laissez-faire — weak by omission. Parecon — untested.

cruxes.title: Labor mobility and exit
cruxes.prompt: Can people leave a firm or jurisdiction, and how do labor markets clear?
cruxes.verdictText: Social democracy — strongest. Laissez-faire, anarcho-capitalism — free formally, uneven in practice. State capitalism — free for citizens, restricted for migrants. Market socialism, social anarchism — admission-dependent. Central planning — worst. Parecon — untested.

cruxes.title: Provision of basic needs and security
cruxes.prompt: How are healthcare, education, housing, and income floors provided?
cruxes.verdictText: Social democracy — strongest. State capitalism — effective where prioritized (Singapore housing), thin elsewhere. Central planning — unreliable. Market socialism — inherits social democracy. Laissez-faire, anarcho-capitalism — weak. Social anarchism — local. Parecon — untested.

cruxes.title: Scale sensitivity
cruxes.prompt: Does it work at 500 people, 5 million, 500 million?
cruxes.verdictText: Laissez-faire, central planning, state capitalism — scale by construction (with information loss). Social democracy — proven to ~100 million. Market socialism, social anarchism — bounded. Anarcho-capitalism, Parecon — unknown, with theoretical reasons for concern.

cruxes.title: Transition path
cruxes.prompt: How do you get there from here without a revolution?
cruxes.verdictText: Social democracy — the only proven peaceful path. Laissez-faire — partial retrenchment only. Market socialism — one serious attempt, defeated. The rest — revolution, dictatorship, or no path.

cruxes.title: External security and defense
cruxes.prompt: Who defends the system from outside coercion?
cruxes.verdictText: Central planning and state capitalism — strongest, at civilian cost. Social democracy, market socialism, laissez-faire — conventional. Social anarchism — weakest with the clearest historical record. Anarcho-capitalism — theoretically unstable. Parecon — unaddressed.

cruxes.title: Robustness to bad actors
cruxes.prompt: What happens when the people running it are self-interested or malicious?
cruxes.verdictText: Social democracy — strongest record. Social anarchism — strong at small scale (Ostrom), none at large. State capitalism — high variance, no guarantee. Market socialism — moderate. Laissez-faire, anarcho-capitalism — weak against dominant private actors. Central planning — worst. Parecon — partial by design, untested.

cells.mechanism: Prices aggregate dispersed knowledge; profit and loss steer resources (Hayek).
cells.breaks: Prices omit externalities; no mechanism for public goods; monopoly and information asymmetry distort the signal.

cells.mechanism: Same price mechanism; the state corrects known distortions and supplies public goods directly.
cells.breaks: Correction is only as good as the regulator; heavily regulated sectors can lose the signal.

cells.mechanism: Price mechanism for goods. Investment allocation is partly administrative (public banks).
cells.breaks: The investment side reintroduces a planning problem; banks must judge projects without a capital market's signal.

cells.mechanism: Input-output tables, quotas, administrative allocation; modern variant runs optimization on large datasets.
cells.breaks: The calculation problem: tacit and real-time knowledge cannot be centrally collected; quota incentives corrupt reported data. Computation addresses volume, not knowledge that only exists once markets generate it.

cells.mechanism: Mutualism: markets plus mutual credit. Non-market variants: federated councils negotiate directly.
cells.breaks: Mutualism inherits the market's gaps; non-market variants face the calculation problem beyond face-to-face scale. Untested long-run.

cells.mechanism: Markets for most goods; the state directs credit and investment into targeted sectors via state banks and industrial policy.
cells.breaks: Works for catch-up (copying a known frontier); picking winners degrades at the frontier (Japan after 1990). State-owned enterprises and local-government investment misallocate (China's property and infrastructure debt).

cells.mechanism: Pure price system, extended to law, courts, and security as purchasable services.
cells.breaks: No mechanism at all for public goods or diffuse externalities; assumes courts and defense behave like ordinary goods.

cells.mechanism: Councils submit consumption and production proposals; facilitation boards compute indicative prices; several rounds of revision converge on a plan.
cells.breaks: Never tested. Critics (Schweickart, "Nonsense on Stilts") argue the iteration burden is enormous and indicative prices without real trades face the same calculation problem. Hahnel has only simulations.

cells.mechanism: Private risk capital; competition selects; bankruptcy clears failures fast.
cells.breaks: Short-termism; under-investment in basic research; winners entrench.

cells.mechanism: Same, plus public basic research and social insurance lowering the personal cost of failure.
cells.breaks: Too-big-to-fail bailouts soften the budget constraint; public R&D can be captured.

cells.mechanism: Firms compete and can fail; public banks fund new ventures.
cells.breaks: Cooperatives have poor access to outside risk capital; federation solidarity funds recreate the soft budget constraint (Fagor, 2013).

cells.mechanism: Directed investment into state priorities; failure is administrative.
cells.breaks: Strong in a few prioritized sectors; stagnant elsewhere; failure is hidden, not cleared (Kornai).

cells.mechanism: Cooperative credit or communal funding; failure borne by the association.
cells.breaks: No scaled evidence; unclear who bears enough concentrated risk for large, long-horizon bets.

cells.mechanism: Massive directed investment plus private competition in non-strategic sectors; export discipline (firms must compete abroad to keep support).
cells.breaks: Excellent for catch-up; frontier innovation is contested — recent Chinese success in EVs, batteries, and solar cuts against the older view that it cannot reach the frontier. Zombie state enterprises persist.

cells.mechanism: Maximal private risk-bearing; no bailouts of any kind.
cells.breaks: No public research at all; same entrenchment problem as laissez-faire with no antitrust remedy.

cells.mechanism: Councils propose investments; workers are paid for effort, not output.
cells.breaks: No risk-bearer; innovation is a collective proposal with no reward for success. Albert addresses this in a chapter; there is no evidence either way.

cells.mechanism: Private ownership; surplus to owners; wage labor as voluntary contract.
cells.breaks: The socialist critique: the wage relation is hierarchical, and surplus accrues to capital regardless of contribution.

cells.mechanism: Private ownership; surplus partly redirected by taxation; codetermination gives voice without ownership.
cells.breaks: Codetermination's measured effects are neutral-to-small-positive; the wage relation is untouched.

cells.mechanism: Workers own or control the firm; profit distributed to members.
cells.breaks: Two-tier workforces in practice (a third of Mondragón's workers are members); members resist new hires.

cells.mechanism: State ownership; workers are employees of the state.
cells.breaks: The state becomes the new owning class (Bakunin's prediction).

cells.mechanism: Collective or communal ownership; no wage labor; distribution by contribution or need.
cells.breaks: Firm-level ownership still fragments production into entitled groups (the anarcho-communist objection).

cells.mechanism: Mixed: private firms, state enterprises, and hybrids; surplus split between private owners and the state; wage labor throughout.
cells.breaks: In China the party retains control rights over large private firms regardless of formal ownership; in Korea, chaebol families control conglomerates through minority stakes.

cells.mechanism: Absolute private ownership including of law and security; wage labor as contract.
cells.breaks: Identical to laissez-faire on this crux; removes even the minimal state's constraints on ownership.

cells.mechanism: Social ownership; no wage labor; remuneration by effort and sacrifice, measured by co-workers.
cells.breaks: Effort is hard to measure and easy to game; balanced job complexes require rotating people out of tasks they are best at.

cells.mechanism: Managerial hierarchy answerable to owners; voice is exit or individual bargaining.
cells.breaks: Firms are internally command-and-control ("islands of tyranny").

cells.mechanism: Hierarchy plus unions, sectoral bargaining, works councils, board seats.
cells.breaks: Voice can be outvoted; union density has fallen outside the Nordics.

cells.mechanism: One member, one vote; elected managers.
cells.breaks: Larger cooperatives drift toward conventional hierarchy; Mondragón splits cooperatives around 400–500 workers.

cells.mechanism: State-appointed management; nominal councils.
cells.breaks: Rigid hierarchy with political oversight; dissent is dangerous.

cells.mechanism: Direct democracy; recallable delegates; bottom-up federation.
cells.breaks: Slow, and thins as groups grow.

cells.mechanism: Managerial hierarchy; unions are state-controlled or party-aligned (China's ACFTU; Singapore's NTUC).
cells.breaks: Voice is weakest of any market system; strikes are suppressed or channeled.

cells.mechanism: Hierarchy by contract; exit only.
cells.breaks: Same as laissez-faire, without even labor law.

cells.mechanism: Balanced job complexes: every worker does a mix of empowering and rote tasks so no "coordinator class" forms; councils decide.
cells.breaks: Its signature idea and its most criticized: rotating experts out of expert work trades competence for equality. Untested.

cells.mechanism: Coasean bargaining, property rights, private provision.
cells.breaks: Bargaining fails for diffuse harms; public goods under-supplied.

cells.mechanism: Pigouvian taxes, cap-and-trade, regulation, direct provision.
cells.breaks: Regulators can be captured; correction lags. Still the best record.

cells.mechanism: Same tools applied to worker-owned firms.
cells.breaks: Co-ops have no inherent incentive to internalize externalities; need the same external correction.

cells.mechanism: Planners can include any cost in principle.
cells.breaks: Worst environmental record of the 20th century in practice (Aral Sea, Soviet-bloc pollution).

cells.mechanism: Communal ownership aligns incentives locally (Ostrom).
cells.breaks: No mechanism for cross-community externalities or continental public goods.

cells.mechanism: The state can act decisively when it prioritizes the problem.
cells.breaks: Acts only when it chooses to: China's air pollution turnaround after 2013 followed three decades of growth-first neglect. No independent check forces the choice.

cells.mechanism: Bargaining and private litigation only.
cells.breaks: No coercive remedy for diffuse harms; the weakest column on this crux.

cells.mechanism: Consumer councils weigh social and environmental impacts in the plan by construction.
cells.breaks: Untested; depends on councils correctly valuing harms with no price benchmark.

cells.mechanism: Competition erodes rents; inheritance disperses fortunes.
cells.breaks: r > g (Piketty): concentration is the default; network effects create durable monopolies.

cells.mechanism: Progressive taxation, inheritance tax, antitrust, codetermination as pre-distribution.
cells.breaks: Wealth taxes mostly repealed in Europe; capital mobility disciplines the taxing state; concentration rose across the OECD after 1980.

cells.mechanism: Structural: no private ownership of large capital.
cells.breaks: Concentration relocates to successful cooperatives and public investment banks.

cells.mechanism: Structural: no private capital.
cells.breaks: Inequality reappears as political privilege (nomenklatura).

cells.mechanism: Structural: no capital ownership, no state.
cells.breaks: Nothing prevents re-concentration except vigilance; no case has run long enough to observe drift.

cells.mechanism: The state can break private concentration at will (Alibaba/Ant, 2020) and owns the commanding heights.
cells.breaks: Concentration sits in the party-state and connected families; crony capitalism (chaebol) is the characteristic failure; the state's own power is unchecked.

cells.mechanism: Nothing structural; competition among protection agencies is supposed to prevent domination.
cells.breaks: Nozick's argument: a dominant protection agency becomes a de facto state. Concentration of coercive capacity is the specific risk.

cells.mechanism: Structural: no capital; balanced job complexes target the "coordinator class" — the technocratic elite that anarchism and Marxism both missed.
cells.breaks: Untested; the coordinator-class analysis is Albert's most distinctive contribution and his answer to why Soviet planning produced a new elite.

cells.mechanism: A small state has little to capture; constitutional limits.
cells.breaks: A weak state is captured by default — it cannot enforce against concentrated private power.

cells.mechanism: Separation of powers, courts, free press, unions as counter-power, transparency. Taxation itself creates an accountability bargain.
cells.breaks: Regulatory capture (Stigler); discretionary spending enables patronage; durability depends on continual re-contestation.

cells.mechanism: Same tools; fewer concentrated private actors.
cells.breaks: Public investment banks are the new capture target (Yugoslav banks were politically directed).

cells.mechanism: None internal; the state is the economy.
cells.breaks: Worst case: no separation of economic and political power; no press or courts.

cells.mechanism: No state to capture; recallable delegates; polycentric governance.
cells.breaks: The crux reappears as defense and re-emergence; nothing structurally prevents a coercive organization from re-forming.

cells.mechanism: Varies entirely with elite discipline: Singapore's low corruption and meritocratic bureaucracy vs. Marcos-era Philippines. Korea and Taiwan later democratized.
cells.breaks: State and capital are fused by design; capture runs both ways. Where elites are undisciplined the result is kleptocracy. No internal mechanism guarantees the Singapore outcome.

cells.mechanism: No state to capture.
cells.breaks: Absent Leviathan: private domination fills the space; protection agencies become warlords or a state (Somalia 1991–2006 is the contested case — Leeson argues outcomes improved vs. the prior regime; others point to warlord rule).

cells.mechanism: No state; facilitation boards and councils.
cells.breaks: Untested; facilitation boards are the obvious capture target and the coordinator-class problem in miniature.

cells.mechanism: Free labor market.
cells.breaks: Non-competes, employer-tied benefits, monopsony.

cells.mechanism: Free labor market plus portable benefits; Nordic "flexicurity."
cells.breaks: Insider/outsider markets where employment protection is high (Southern Europe).

cells.mechanism: Workers choose firms but must be admitted; capital accounts pay out slowly; federations reassign internally.
cells.breaks: Admission friction, golden handcuffs, mobility bounded by the federation.

cells.mechanism: Administrative assignment; internal passports.
cells.breaks: Workers often could not legally change cities; emigration criminalized.

cells.mechanism: Free association.
cells.breaks: Admission-dependent; same dilution logic as cooperatives.

cells.mechanism: Labor markets mostly free; heavy reliance on migrant and guest labor.
cells.breaks: China's hukou system restricts internal migration and excludes migrants from urban services; Singapore's guest-worker regime ties residence to employer.

cells.mechanism: Free by contract.
cells.breaks: Same as laissez-faire; contracts can restrict exit with no labor law to limit them.

cells.mechanism: Council membership; job complexes assigned within councils.
cells.breaks: Movement between councils requires re-balancing job complexes; friction likely. Untested.

cells.mechanism: Market provision, charity, insurance.
cells.breaks: Systematic under-provision for those who cannot pay; adverse selection.

cells.mechanism: Universal tax-funded provision plus social insurance.
cells.breaks: Cost growth; the state becomes a large provider (the discretion concern). Strongest outcome record.

cells.mechanism: Assumes a social-democratic welfare state on top.
cells.breaks: Adds nothing beyond social democracy here.

cells.mechanism: Universal state provision by construction.
cells.breaks: Chronic shortage: guaranteed on paper, unreliable in practice; famine when the plan fails.

cells.mechanism: Communal provision; mutual aid societies.
cells.breaks: Community scale only.

cells.mechanism: Targeted, often through mandatory savings (Singapore's CPF) and state housing (HDB houses ~80% of Singaporeans); China expanded basic insurance after 2003.
cells.breaks: Korea and Taiwan built welfare states only after democratizing; China's provision is thin outside cities. Coverage follows state priority, not citizen entitlement.

cells.mechanism: Charity and insurance only.
cells.breaks: Weakest column; no mechanism for those who cannot pay.

cells.mechanism: Consumption councils allocate by need within the plan.
cells.breaks: Untested.

cells.mechanism: 19th-century Britain and U.S.; no modern pure case.
cells.breaks: Rapid growth alongside severe inequality and instability; every modern economy moved away from it.

cells.mechanism: Nordics since the 1930s; Germany since 1951; most of the OECD partially.
cells.breaks: Consistently high on freedom, health, mobility, innovation. Transferability contested.

cells.mechanism: Yugoslavia 1950–90; Mondragón since 1956; thousands of cooperatives.
cells.breaks: Co-ops match conventional productivity; Yugoslavia collapsed with its state; Mondragón reverts to capitalism abroad. No national case outlasting its regime.

cells.mechanism: USSR 1928–91; China 1949–78; Eastern bloc; Cuba; North Korea.
cells.breaks: Industrialization in priorities; shortage, stagnation, famine; every case liberalized or collapsed.

cells.mechanism: Spain 1936–39; Ukraine 1918–21; Rojava since 2012; Ostrom's commons; Zapatistas.
cells.breaks: Functional locally under wartime conditions; destroyed externally each time; no peacetime long-run test.

cells.mechanism: Japan 1950–90; Korea, Taiwan, Singapore since the 1960s; China since 1978.
cells.breaks: The strongest growth record of the last sixty years; Korea and Taiwan democratized, Singapore and China did not. The one system on this list whose track record is mostly positive and mostly recent.

cells.mechanism: No case. Medieval Iceland (930–1262) and Somalia 1991–2006 as contested analogies.
cells.breaks: Iceland's system ended in civil war and Norwegian rule; Somalia's outcome is disputed (Leeson vs. critics). No modern evidence.

cells.mechanism: No case. Small collectives (South End Press, Z Magazine).
cells.breaks: Nothing beyond a handful of workplaces.

cells.mechanism: Prices scale without limit; that is the point of the price mechanism.
cells.breaks: Public-goods and externality failures grow with scale (climate).

cells.mechanism: Scales via bureaucracy and law; the Nordics are 5–10 million each, Germany 84 million.
cells.breaks: Trust and homogeneity questions at U.S. or Indian scale; the largest social democracies are the most contested.

cells.mechanism: Individual cooperatives cap around 500 (Mondragón splits them); federations reach ~80,000.
cells.breaks: No national-scale case; the federation's own size bounds mobility and capital pooling.

cells.mechanism: Scales administratively — the USSR planned for 290 million.
cells.breaks: Information degrades with every layer of hierarchy; the calculation problem is a scale problem.

cells.mechanism: Strong at village, factory, and commons scale (Ostrom's cases are hundreds to thousands).
cells.breaks: Direct democracy and face-to-face trust do not survive scale; regional coordination in Spain was contested.

cells.mechanism: Scales to 1.4 billion (China) through state capacity.
cells.breaks: Local-government incentive distortion at scale (GDP-target gaming, debt); the center loses information the same way planners do.

cells.mechanism: Unknown; theory assumes competition among agencies at any scale.
cells.breaks: No evidence; agency competition at continental scale is speculation.

cells.mechanism: Planning rounds are combinatorial: every council's proposal affects every other's.
cells.breaks: The iteration burden grows faster than population; the strongest theoretical objection to the model.

cells.mechanism: Deregulation and retrenchment (Thatcher, Reagan, Pinochet's Chile).
cells.breaks: Politically hard to sustain; every attempt stopped well short of the model.

cells.mechanism: Incremental, electoral, proven repeatedly (New Deal, postwar Europe, Nordic reforms).
cells.breaks: Can be reversed incrementally too; the path is real but never finished.

cells.mechanism: Schweickart assumes a "landslide election." Wright's "interstitial" strategy: grow the co-op sector until it is dominant. Sweden's 1976 Meidner Plan (wage-earner funds buying into firms) was the serious attempt.
cells.breaks: Meidner was defeated politically and dismantled by 1991; co-op share of most economies has stayed small for a century.

cells.mechanism: Revolution or conquest in every historical case.
cells.breaks: No electoral path exists; the transitions were violent.

cells.mechanism: Revolution (Spain, Ukraine) or prefiguration (build the new inside the old).
cells.breaks: Revolutionary cases were destroyed; prefigurative cases stay small.

cells.mechanism: Arose under authoritarian regimes facing security threats (Korea, Taiwan, Singapore) or after a prior collapse (China).
cells.breaks: No democratic society has adopted it deliberately; the path ran through dictatorship.

cells.mechanism: Secession, seasteading, charter cities, "startup societies."
cells.breaks: No path from an existing state; charter-city attempts (Honduras) were reversed.

cells.mechanism: Prefigurative: build participatory workplaces and councils.
cells.breaks: No path proposed beyond example-setting.

cells.mechanism: The minimal state's one uncontested function.
cells.breaks: Defense is a public good the model otherwise disclaims; large militaries create the state the model wants to limit.

cells.mechanism: Conventional state defense; alliances (NATO, Nordic cooperation).
cells.breaks: Small states depend on alliances; defense spending competes with the welfare state.

cells.mechanism: State defense.
cells.breaks: Same as social democracy.

cells.mechanism: Strong: the USSR won the Eastern Front and matched the U.S. militarily for forty years.
cells.breaks: Militarization consumed the civilian economy; defense was the one sector planning served well and at everything else's expense.

cells.mechanism: Militias; federated defense.
cells.breaks: Spain's militias were absorbed into the Republican army then crushed; Makhno was crushed; Rojava survives on external patrons. The weakest column.

cells.mechanism: Strong: the developmental state is partly a security state (Korea, Taiwan, Singapore all built under existential threat).
cells.breaks: Security justification underwrites the authoritarianism.

cells.mechanism: Private defense agencies.
cells.breaks: The standard objection (Nozick): a successful agency becomes a state; an unsuccessful one loses to a state.

cells.mechanism: Unaddressed in the model.
Competition disciplines firms; a small state has little to abuse.
cells.breaks: A weak state cannot stop a private actor who achieves dominance; fraud and coercion go unremedied.

cells.mechanism: Checks and balances, courts, press, elections; the Nordics' record of resisting corruption is the best available.
cells.breaks: Capture is slow degradation, not a coup; institutions decay when not defended (the "narrow corridor" is narrow).

cells.mechanism: Cooperative governance: elected, recallable management.
cells.breaks: Elected managers entrench like any politician; public investment banks concentrate discretion.

cells.mechanism: None above the top.
cells.breaks: Stalin and Mao: the worst outcomes in the whole table came from unconstrained leaders inside this system.

cells.mechanism: Recallable delegates; Ostrom's commons rely on monitoring and graduated sanctions, designed for exactly this at small scale.
cells.breaks: No answer to an armed faction at any scale; Spain's own revolution saw anarchists fighting communists in Barcelona (May 1937).

cells.mechanism: Depends entirely on elite discipline and succession; Singapore built institutions to enforce it (high official pay, anti-corruption agency).
cells.breaks: The Marcos, Suharto, and post-Soviet cases show the same structure producing kleptocracy; succession is the recurring crisis (China's is unresolved).

cells.mechanism: Competing agencies check each other.
cells.breaks: A dominant agency faces no check; the model assumes competition persists without an enforcer of competition.

cells.mechanism: Balanced job complexes and recallable councils prevent a coordinator class.
cells.breaks: Designed against elite formation, not against coercion; unaddressed for armed or fraudulent actors.

sourceCandidates.title: Federalist Nos
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Madison — Federalist Nos. 10 and 51 (1787–88).** Short. Factions, and the original "ambition must be made to counteract ambition."

sourceCandidates.author: Hirschman
sourceCandidates.title: Exit, Voice, and Loyalty (1970)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Hirschman — *Exit, Voice, and Loyalty* (1970).** Short. When exit disciplines power and when it just lets it escape.

sourceCandidates.title: The Calculus of Consent (1962)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Buchanan & Tullock — *The Calculus of Consent* (1962).** Public choice: models officials as self-interested and asks which constitutional rules survive that assumption. The intellectual home of the government-tyranny worry.

sourceCandidates.author: Ostrom
sourceCandidates.title: Governing the Commons (1990)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **▶ Ostrom — *Governing the Commons* (1990).** Nobel-winning fieldwork on communities managing shared resources without privatization or central control.

sourceCandidates.author: James C
sourceCandidates.title: James C
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **▶ James C. Scott — *Seeing Like a State* (1998).** Why top-down "legibility" schemes fail; written by an anarchist-sympathetic political scientist, so it bridges to the anarchist section. Belongs equally under the calculation debate — it is about planning failure.

sourceCandidates.author: Besley & Persson
sourceCandidates.title: Pillars of Prosperity (2011)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Besley & Persson — *Pillars of Prosperity* (2011).** State capacity as a development achievement; why weak states are often more predatory.

sourceCandidates.author: Stigler
sourceCandidates.title: The Theory of Economic Regulation (1971)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Stigler — "The Theory of Economic Regulation" (1971).** Short article. The foundational regulatory-capture argument.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Power, institutions, and the state/society problem
sourceCandidates.author: Hall & Soskice (eds.)
sourceCandidates.title: Varieties of Capitalism (2001)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Hall & Soskice (eds.) — *Varieties of Capitalism* (2001).** The "coordinated vs. liberal market economies" framework; the academic basis for treating Germany and the Nordics as a distinct system.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Power, institutions, and the state/society problem
sourceCandidates.author: Hayek
sourceCandidates.title: The Road to Serfdom (1944) and Friedman — Capitalism and Freedom (1962)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Hayek — *The Road to Serfdom* (1944)** and **Friedman — *Capitalism and Freedom* (1962).** The canonical statements of the taxation-and-tyranny worry; the laissez-faire side of the argument.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Power, institutions, and the state/society problem
sourceCandidates.author: Coase & Wang
sourceCandidates.title: How China Became Capitalist (2012)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Coase & Wang — *How China Became Capitalist* (2012).** The state-capitalism / developmental-state case, from the author of "The Nature of the Firm."

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Markets, planning, and the calculation debate
sourceCandidates.author: Hayek
sourceCandidates.title: The Use of Knowledge in Society (1945)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **▶ Hayek — "The Use of Knowledge in Society" (1945).** ~15 pages. The whole knowledge-problem argument.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Markets, planning, and the calculation debate
sourceCandidates.author: Mises
sourceCandidates.title: Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth (1920)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Mises — "Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth" (1920).** The original salvo.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Markets, planning, and the calculation debate
sourceCandidates.author: Coase
sourceCandidates.title: The Nature of the Firm (1937)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Coase — "The Nature of the Firm" (1937).** Short. Islands of planning in a sea of markets.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Markets, planning, and the calculation debate
sourceCandidates.author: Kornai
sourceCandidates.title: The Socialist System (1992)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Kornai — *The Socialist System* (1992).** The soft-budget-constraint account from inside actually-existing planning.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Markets, planning, and the calculation debate
sourceCandidates.author: Alec Nove
sourceCandidates.title: The Economics of Feasible Socialism (1983)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **▶ Alec Nove — *The Economics of Feasible Socialism* (1983).** A socialist who took the calculation problem seriously and designed around it.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Markets, planning, and the calculation debate
sourceCandidates.author: Schumpeter
sourceCandidates.title: Capitalism, Socialism, and Democracy (1942)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Schumpeter — *Capitalism, Socialism, and Democracy* (1942).** Creative destruction, plus an even-handed narration of the debate.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Markets, planning, and the calculation debate
sourceCandidates.author: Phillips & Rozworski
sourceCandidates.title: The People's Republic of Walmart (2019)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Phillips & Rozworski — *The People's Republic of Walmart* (2019).** The modern pro-planning case built on corporate logistics.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Markets, planning, and the calculation debate
sourceCandidates.author: Cockshott & Cottrell
sourceCandidates.title: Towards a New Socialism (1993)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Cockshott & Cottrell — *Towards a New Socialism* (1993).** The computational-planning proposal.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Economic democracy, market socialism, worker ownership
sourceCandidates.author: Schweickart
sourceCandidates.title: After Capitalism (2002)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **▶ Schweickart — *After Capitalism* (2002).** The Economic Democracy model: worker self-management, markets for goods, socially controlled investment.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Economic democracy, market socialism, worker ownership
sourceCandidates.author: Erik Olin Wright
sourceCandidates.title: Envisioning Real Utopias (2010)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **▶ Erik Olin Wright — *Envisioning Real Utopias* (2010).** The best survey of real-world experiments (Mondragón, participatory budgeting, Wikipedia, basic income) with honest assessment of each.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Economic democracy, market socialism, worker ownership
sourceCandidates.author: Robert Dahl
sourceCandidates.title: A Preface to Economic Democracy (1985)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Robert Dahl — *A Preface to Economic Democracy* (1985).** Short. The political-theory case that democratic principles apply to firms.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Economic democracy, market socialism, worker ownership
sourceCandidates.author: Whyte & Whyte
sourceCandidates.title: Making Mondragon (1988)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Whyte & Whyte — *Making Mondragon* (1988).** The definitive institutional history; explains the capital-account mechanics.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Economic democracy, market socialism, worker ownership
sourceCandidates.author: David Ellerman
sourceCandidates.title: The Democratic Worker-Owned Firm (1990)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **David Ellerman — *The Democratic Worker-Owned Firm* (1990).** The "labor theory of property" argument against the employment contract itself.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Economic democracy, market socialism, worker ownership
sourceCandidates.author: Isabelle Ferreras
sourceCandidates.title: Firms as Political Entities (2017)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Isabelle Ferreras — *Firms as Political Entities* (2017).** "Economic bicameralism": a workers' chamber alongside the shareholders' chamber. The most developed extension of codetermination.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Economic democracy, market socialism, worker ownership
sourceCandidates.author: John Roemer
sourceCandidates.title: A Future for Socialism (1994)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **John Roemer — *A Future for Socialism* (1994).** A different market-socialist design (coupon-based shares), for contrast with Schweickart.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Economic democracy, market socialism, worker ownership
sourceCandidates.author: Michael Albert
sourceCandidates.title: Parecon: Life After Capitalism (2003)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Michael Albert — *Parecon: Life After Capitalism* (2003).** Participatory economics; the main non-market democratic proposal. (Albert is sole author; Hahnel co-wrote the earlier academic statements, *The Political Economy of Participatory Economics* and *Looking Forward*, both 1991.) Pair with Schweickart's 2006 critique, "Nonsense on Stilts: Michael Albert's Parecon" — a direct market-socialist vs. non-market exchange.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Economic democracy, market socialism, worker ownership
sourceCandidates.author: Blasi, Freeman & Kruse
sourceCandidates.title: The Citizen's Share (2013)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Blasi, Freeman & Kruse — *The Citizen's Share* (2013).** Empirical record of employee ownership in the U.S.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Economic democracy, market socialism, worker ownership
sourceCandidates.author: Richard Wolff
sourceCandidates.title: Democracy at Work (2012)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Richard Wolff — *Democracy at Work* (2012).** Accessible; worker self-directed enterprises.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Economic democracy, market socialism, worker ownership
sourceCandidates.author: Jäger & Noy
sourceCandidates.title: What Does Codetermination Do? (NBER Working Paper 28921, 2021)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Jäger & Noy — "What Does Codetermination Do?" (NBER Working Paper 28921, 2021).** The empirical basis for the codetermination claims in Part 1.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Economic democracy, market socialism, worker ownership
sourceCandidates.author: Pérotin
sourceCandidates.title: What do we really know about worker co-operatives? (Co-operatives UK, 2016)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Pérotin — "What do we really know about worker co-operatives?" (Co-operatives UK, 2016).** The productivity meta-review cited in Part 1.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Economic democracy, market socialism, worker ownership
sourceCandidates.author: Hacker
sourceCandidates.title: The Institutional Foundations of Middle-Class Democracy (Policy Network, 2011)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Hacker — "The Institutional Foundations of Middle-Class Democracy" (Policy Network, 2011).** Where "predistribution" was coined.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Anarchist
sourceCandidates.author: Proudhon
sourceCandidates.title: What Is Property? (1840)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Proudhon — *What Is Property?* (1840).** The mutualist foundation; possession vs. property.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Anarchist
sourceCandidates.author: Kropotkin
sourceCandidates.title: The Conquest of Bread (1892) and Mutual Aid (1902)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Kropotkin — *The Conquest of Bread* (1892) and *Mutual Aid* (1902).** Anarcho-communism; *Mutual Aid* argues cooperation, not just competition, drives evolution and social order — it supports the anarchist premise rather than describing the system.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Anarchist
sourceCandidates.author: Bakunin
sourceCandidates.title: Statism and Anarchy (1873)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Bakunin — *Statism and Anarchy* (1873).** The collectivist critique of Marx, including the prediction that a "workers' state" becomes a new ruling class.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Anarchist
sourceCandidates.author: Rudolf Rocker
sourceCandidates.title: Anarcho-Syndicalism: Theory and Practice (1938)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Rudolf Rocker — *Anarcho-Syndicalism: Theory and Practice* (1938).** The standard statement.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Anarchist
sourceCandidates.author: Colin Ward
sourceCandidates.title: Anarchy in Action (1973)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **▶ Colin Ward — *Anarchy in Action* (1973).** Short, practical; treats anarchism as already present in how people organize. Good fit for an engineering mindset.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Anarchist
sourceCandidates.author: James C
sourceCandidates.title: James C
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **James C. Scott — *Two Cheers for Anarchism* (2012).** Short essays; the "two cheers" hedge is honest about limits.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Anarchist
sourceCandidates.author: Kevin Carson
sourceCandidates.title: Organization Theory: A Libertarian Perspective (2008)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **▶ Kevin Carson — *Organization Theory: A Libertarian Perspective* (2008).** A mutualist applying the Coase firm-size question to argue that state intervention subsidizes firms beyond their efficient scale. Directly relevant to the concentration thread. *Note:* self-published (BookSurge, Center for a Stateless Society) by an independent scholar — a serious argument, not a peer-reviewed authority.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Anarchist
sourceCandidates.author: Sam Dolgoff (ed.)
sourceCandidates.title: The Anarchist Collectives (1974)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Sam Dolgoff (ed.) — *The Anarchist Collectives* (1974).** Primary documents from Spain 1936–39, the only large-scale test.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Anarchist
sourceCandidates.author: Murray Bookchin
sourceCandidates.title: The Next Revolution (2015)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Murray Bookchin — *The Next Revolution* (2015).** Libertarian municipalism; the theoretical basis for Rojava's confederalism. *Note:* Bookchin broke with anarchism in 1999 and called his later politics "Communalism"; this posthumous collection is mostly post-break essays. Adjacent to anarchism rather than inside it.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Anarchist
sourceCandidates.author: Graeber & Wengrow
sourceCandidates.title: The Dawn of Everything (2021)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Graeber & Wengrow — *The Dawn of Everything* (2021).** Argues the archaeological record shows far more variety in political organization than "state or chaos" allows. Anthropology by anarchists, not anarchist theory — background, not a statement of the tradition.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Anarchist
sourceCandidates.author: Ruth Kinna
sourceCandidates.title: The Government of No One (2019)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Ruth Kinna — *The Government of No One* (2019).** A modern scholarly map of the tradition before diving into primary sources.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Concentration, capture, and the fixes
sourceCandidates.author: Piketty
sourceCandidates.title: Capital in the Twenty-First Century (2014)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Piketty — *Capital in the Twenty-First Century* (2014).** The r > g argument for why concentration is the default.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Concentration, capture, and the fixes
sourceCandidates.author: Tim Wu
sourceCandidates.title: The Curse of Bigness (2018)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **▶ Tim Wu — *The Curse of Bigness* (2018).** Short. The neo-Brandeisian case that concentration is a political problem, not just a price problem.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Concentration, capture, and the fixes
sourceCandidates.author: Lina Khan
sourceCandidates.title: Amazon's Antitrust Paradox (2017, Yale Law Journal)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Lina Khan — "Amazon's Antitrust Paradox" (2017, *Yale Law Journal*).** The article that relaunched the antitrust debate.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Concentration, capture, and the fixes
sourceCandidates.author: Henry George
sourceCandidates.title: Progress and Poverty (1879)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Henry George — *Progress and Poverty* (1879).** The land-value-tax argument; the core is in the first third.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Concentration, capture, and the fixes
sourceCandidates.author: Ackerman & Alstott
sourceCandidates.title: The Stakeholder Society (1999)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Ackerman & Alstott — *The Stakeholder Society* (1999).** Universal basic capital.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Concentration, capture, and the fixes
sourceCandidates.author: Lessig
sourceCandidates.title: Republic, Lost (2011)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Lessig — *Republic, Lost* (2011).** Money in politics as systemic rather than individual corruption.

sourceCandidates.sectionTitle: Concentration, capture, and the fixes
sourceCandidates.author: Landemore
sourceCandidates.title: Open Democracy (2020)
sourceCandidates.rawMarkdown: **Landemore — *Open Democracy* (2020).** The strongest case for sortition and citizens' assemblies as capture-resistant institutions.
